mn2:1.2: At one time the Buddha was living at Sāvatthi, in Jeta’s grove, at Anāthapiṇḍika's park.
mn2:1.3: There the Buddha addressed the monks:
mn2:1.5: “Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha.
mn2:2.1: “Monks, I will teach you how to control every vice.
mn2:2.2: Listen to this and carefully apply your mind to it; I will speak.”
mn2:2.3: “Yes, Bhante,” those monks replied to the Buddha.
mn2:3.1: “Monks, I say that the elimination of vices is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.
mn2:3.2: For one who knows and sees what?
mn2:3.3: Application of mind based on an understanding of causality, and application of mind not based on an understanding of causality.
mn2:3.4: Monks, when one applies one’s mind without an understanding of causality, one develops new vices, and one’s old vices grow stronger.
mn2:3.5: Monks, when one applies one’s mind based on an understanding of causality, one does not develop new vices, and one’s old vices are abandoned.
mn2:4.1: Monks, there are vices to be abandoned by seeing, vices to be abandoned by self-control, vices to be abandoned by using, vices to be abandoned by enduring, vices to be abandoned by avoiding, vices to be abandoned by removing, and vices to be abandoned by developing.
mn2:5.0: Vices to be Abandoned by Seeing
mn2:5.1: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by seeing?
mn2:5.2: In this case, monks, an uneducated commoner—one who does not see noble people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of noble people, and who does not see good people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of good people—
mn2:5.3: does not understand what the mind the should not be applied to and what the mind should be applied to.
mn2:5.4: Since they do not understand what the mind should be applied and what the mind should not be applied to, they apply their mind to what they should not apply it to and they do not apply their mind to what they should apply it to.
mn2:6.1: And, monks, what should the mind not be applied to that they apply their mind to?
mn2:6.2: Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, causes a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to grow stronger;
mn2:6.3: or causes a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to grow stronger;
mn2:6.4: or causes a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to grow stronger;
mn2:6.5: this is what the mind should not be applied to that they apply their mind to.
mn2:6.6: And, monks, what should the mind be applied to that they do not apply their mind to?
mn2:6.7: Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, does not cause a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to be abandoned;
mn2:6.8: or does not cause a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to be abandoned;
mn2:6.9: or does not cause a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to be abandoned;
mn2:6.10: this is what the mind should be applied to that they do not apply their mind to.
mn2:7.1: So when they apply their mind to that which it should not be applied to and do not apply their mind to that which it should be applied to, they develop new vices and their old vices grow stronger.
mn2:7.2: This is how they apply their mind without an understanding of causality:
mn2:7.3: they think, ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having done what, what did I become in the past?’
mn2:7.4: ‘Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having done what, what will I become in the future?’
mn2:7.5: Or they are confused about the present:
mn2:7.6: ‘Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go from here?’
mn2:8.1: When one applies one’s mind in this way, one of six beliefs arises:
mn2:8.2: The belief ‘I have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain.
mn2:8.3: Or the belief ‘I do not have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain.
mn2:8.4: Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.
mn2:8.5: Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive what is not the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.
mn2:8.6: Or the belief ‘Using what is not the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.
mn2:8.8: ‘This is my soul; it speaks, it feels, it experiences the results of good and evil actions; and this soul of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and will remain like this for eternity.’
mn2:8.9: Monks, this is called settling on a belief, becoming entangled in a belief, becoming disturbed by a belief, becoming agitated by a belief, becoming fettered by a belief.
mn2:8.10: Fettered by a belief, monks, the uneducated commoner is not freed from birth, decrepitude, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and anguish;
mn2:8.11: they are not freed from suffering, I say.
mn2:9.1: Monks, an educated disciple of the noble ones—
